stem: Sales of HomeFax's desktop fax machines are falling as businesses switch to e-signatures. Two rivals have exited the market, HomeFax has cut its line to its two best sellers, and it sells them at very low prices through fewer retailers with no advertising. Which PLC stage is this?
options: Maturity
Decline
Growth
Introduction
explanation: Sales falling because of a new technology, competitors exiting, a line trimmed to best sellers, very low prices, fewer retailers and no advertising are all decline entries in Figure 8-3. Maturity also involves price pressure, but there discounts are frequent while distribution stays full.

stem: Sales in the decline stage typically fall because of environmental change or new technology, such as the arrival of a better substitute.
options: True
False
explanation: True. Decline is usually triggered by outside change, such as streaming replacing DVDs. This differs from cannibalization, where the firm's own new product takes sales from its existing products.

stem: Both the introduction and decline stages can show relatively few competitors and minimal profits. Which pair of cues tells them apart?
options: Introduction: few competitors exist; decline: some competitors are leaving
Introduction: limited distribution; decline: full distribution
Introduction: very low prices; decline: skimming prices
Introduction: brand loyalty objective; decline: awareness objective
explanation: Introduction has few competitors because the market is new; decline has reduced competition because rivals are leaving a shrinking market. The distribution option is wrong because decline has REDUCED distribution, not full distribution.

stem: Skyline Audio's portable CD players are in the decline stage. Following Figure 8-3, what should its product strategy be?
options: Introduce more features to differentiate from rivals
Ensure the full product line is available and innovative
Retain only the best sellers or discontinue the line
Focus on launching the product as a new brand
explanation: Figure 8-3's decline product entry is 'retain only best sellers or discontinue', matching the product rationalization objective. Ensuring a full, innovative line is the maturity entry, and introducing more features is the growth entry.

stem: Which practice is NOT part of the decline stage in Figure 8-3?
options: Very low prices on the remaining items
Distribution reduced to fewer retailers
Frequent price discounts to build brand loyalty
Only minimal promotion, if any at all
explanation: Frequent price discounts aimed at brand loyalty are maturity tactics. In decline, prices are very low, distribution is reduced and promotion is minimal, if any, because the objective is product rationalization.

stem: Simon Watercraft expects, and starts to see, decreasing profits for its product line of water ski boats. In response, the company drastically reduces promotional activities to maximize the remaining profit from the remaining sales. This strategy is known as:
options: line extension
radical innovation
harvesting
commercialization
explanation: Harvesting means keeping the product but reducing marketing support to reap some minor profits during the decline stage, which is exactly what Simon does by slashing promotion. A line extension adds a new item to a line, the opposite of cutting support.

stem: Dropping a product from the company's product line is called:
options: deletion
harvesting
trading down
cannibalization
explanation: Deletion removes the product from the line entirely. Harvesting is the tempting distractor, but harvesting KEEPS the product and simply cuts its marketing support.

stem: Maple Grove Foods discontinues its canned lima beans and removes them from its catalogue so it can put those resources into its growing frozen-meal line. This decline-stage strategy is:
options: harvesting
trading down
market modification
deletion
explanation: Discontinuing a product and removing it from the line is deletion. Harvesting would keep the lima beans on sale with reduced marketing support to collect the remaining profit.

stem: What is the key difference between harvesting and deletion?
options: Harvesting keeps the product but cuts support; deletion drops it from the line
Harvesting drops the product; deletion keeps it with reduced support
Harvesting is used in the maturity stage; deletion is used in the growth stage
Harvesting adds new varieties to the line; deletion removes the old varieties
explanation: Both are decline-stage strategies: harvesting keeps the product and reduces marketing support to reap minor profits, while deletion removes it from the line. The option claiming harvesting drops the product simply reverses the two definitions, a common mix-up.

stem: Why might a firm choose harvesting rather than deletion for a declining product?
options: Harvesting revives sales growth by repositioning the product for new buyers
Some loyal buyers remain, so cutting costs still yields minor profits from remaining sales
Harvesting is a required step before a product can be test marketed again
Deletion is only allowed for products that never reached the maturity stage
explanation: Harvesting makes sense when enough buyers remain that a low-cost, low-support product still throws off some profit. It does not revive sales; reviving sales is the goal of PLC extension strategies such as repositioning.

stem: Brava Cosmetics is harvesting its old line of compact powder. Which action would be INCONSISTENT with a harvesting strategy?
options: Cutting its advertising budget to almost nothing
Keeping the product available for loyal buyers
Reducing the number of retailers that carry it
Launching a national ad campaign to revive sales
explanation: Harvesting means reducing marketing support, so a national campaign to revive sales contradicts it (that would be an attempt to extend the PLC). Cutting ads, keeping the product for loyal buyers and trimming distribution all fit harvesting.

stem: When the Swiffer Sweeper was first introduced it required consumers to understand the new product, how to use it, and what to do with their old brooms and mops. This is an example of a _____ product.
options: learning
new concept
fad
high-learning
explanation: A high-learning product has an extended introductory period because significant effort is required to educate consumers on its usage and benefits, exactly the Swiffer Sweeper situation. A fad is wrong because a fad is defined by a rapid rise and rapid fall, not by consumer education.

stem: A product that requires significant consumer education, and therefore has an extended introductory period, is a:
options: high-learning product
low-learning product
fashion product
minor innovation
explanation: That is the definition of a high-learning product. A low-learning product is the opposite: its benefits are self-evident, so the introduction is short and sales begin immediately.

stem: When induction cooktops first appeared in Canadian stores, buyers had to learn that only magnetic pans work, how the touch controls respond and why the surface stays cool. Sales took years to build. In PLC terms, induction cooktops were a:
options: fad
low-learning product
high-learning product
fashion product
explanation: Needing to learn about new cookware, controls and benefits stretched out the introductory period, the mark of a high-learning product. A low-learning product would have sold immediately because its benefits are self-evident.

stem: The Swiffer Sweeper is a classic high-learning product, yet Figure 8-5 lists the Swiffer WetJet as a continuous innovation. How can both classifications be valid?
options: High-learning is a PLC shape (long introduction); continuous innovation rates how much routines change
They contradict each other, so the WetJet must really be classed as a radical innovation
High-learning and continuous innovation are simply two names for the same concept
High-learning refers to the firm's own production learning curve, not to consumers
explanation: The two frameworks answer different questions. High- vs low-learning describes the SHAPE of the PLC (how long introduction lasts), while minor/continuous/radical classifies the innovation by how much consumer learning it involves; changing routines without totally new learning is continuous. They are not synonyms.

stem: Vireo Mobility is launching a home exoskeleton that users must learn to put on, calibrate and trust before they will rely on it. What PLC pattern should Vireo plan for?
options: Immediate sales with very little promotion needed
A rapid rise in sales followed by a rapid fall
Sales that rise, fade away and return in later cycles
An extended introductory period requiring heavy consumer education
explanation: A product that requires significant consumer learning is a high-learning product, so Vireo should budget for a long introduction stage focused on education. Immediate sales with little promotion describes a low-learning product.

stem: Dr. Oetker, a popular frozen pizza brand, regularly adds new pizza types and flavours to its existing product mix. Most new pizza products begin selling well immediately with very little promotion or communication about the product. In terms of a product life cycle, the lack of promotion is similar to a _____ product.
options: high-learning
fashion
low-learning
concept
explanation: A low-learning product has a short introductory stage because its benefits are self-evident and very little learning is required, so sales start right away with little promotion. High-learning is the opposite: an extended introduction because consumers must be educated.

stem: Which description fits a low-learning product?
options: Significant consumer education is required, so the introduction is extended
Benefits are self-evident, little learning is required, and sales begin immediately
Popularity rises, declines and reappears over the years
Sales rise rapidly and then fall just as rapidly
explanation: A low-learning product's benefits are obvious, so its introduction is short and sales start immediately. An extended introduction with heavy education describes a high-learning product, while cyclical returns and a rapid rise-and-fall describe fashions and fads.

stem: Why is strong distribution especially important for a low-learning product?
options: It is easily copied, so the firm must reach many buyers quickly before imitators do
Consumers need personal selling to understand how to use it
Its sales return in cycles, so stores must restock it every few years
Test marketing is required before it can be sold nationally
explanation: Because a low-learning product is simple to understand, it is also simple for competitors to copy, so the firm needs broad distribution fast to capture sales first. Personal selling to explain usage fits radical or high-learning products, not low-learning ones.

stem: Which pair correctly contrasts low-learning and high-learning products?
options: Low-learning: an extended introduction; high-learning: a short introduction
Low-learning: a rapid rise and fall; high-learning: cyclical returns
Low: short introduction, immediate sales; high: extended introduction, heavy education
Low-learning: a radical innovation; high-learning: a minor innovation
explanation: Low-learning products sell immediately because their benefits are self-evident; high-learning products need an extended introduction to educate consumers. The option giving low-learning the extended introduction reverses them, and the others confuse PLC shapes with fads, fashions and degrees of innovation.

stem: Pantry Pals is launching a new cookie flavour under its well-established brand. Which PLC pattern and priority should it plan for?
options: A short introduction with immediate sales, so secure strong distribution quickly
A long introduction, so invest in personal selling to educate consumers
A cyclical pattern, so plan to relaunch the flavour in ten years
A slow start, so delay distribution until awareness builds
explanation: A new flavour under a known brand is a low-learning product: buyers understand it instantly, so sales start right away, and because it is easy to copy, strong distribution matters. A long, education-heavy introduction would describe a high-learning product.

stem: In 2017, fidget spinners went from unknown to sold in nearly every corner store within months, then almost vanished a year later. In PLC terms, fidget spinners were a:
options: fashion product
fad
low-learning product
high-learning product
explanation: A fad has a rapid rise and an equally rapid fall, giving it a very short life, exactly the fidget-spinner pattern. A fashion product would come back into style in later years, which fidget spinners did not.

stem: Wide-leg jeans were popular in the 1970s, faded, returned in the late 1990s, faded again, and are popular once more. This PLC pattern describes a:
options: fashion product
fad
high-learning product
low-learning product
explanation: A fashion product is a style that becomes popular, declines and then returns in cycles over the years. A fad rises and falls quickly and does not keep coming back.

stem: What distinguishes a fashion product from a fad?
options: A fashion rises and falls rapidly; a fad keeps returning in cycles over the years
A fashion requires heavy consumer education; a fad requires almost none
A fashion is a radical innovation; a fad is usually just a minor innovation
A fashion returns in cycles over the years; a fad rises and falls fast with a very short life
explanation: Fashions are cyclical (they return), while fads are brief (fast up, fast down). The option saying a fashion rises and falls rapidly swaps the two definitions, and the others confuse PLC shapes with learning or innovation categories.

stem: A product with a rapid rise and an equally rapid fall in sales, giving it a very short life cycle, is called a(n) _____.
options: fad
fashion
low-learning product
minor innovation
explanation: That is a fad. A fashion also loses popularity, but it returns in cycles over the years instead of disappearing after one quick spike.

stem: Blitz Toys expects its viral plush toy to be a fad. Which plan best fits that PLC shape?
options: Invest in a long consumer-education campaign before sales take off
Plan to relaunch the toy every decade when the style returns
Produce cautiously and sell fast, avoiding big long-term inventory commitments
Harvest the toy for several years to milk a loyal customer base
explanation: A fad's sales rise and fall rapidly, so the firm should move fast and avoid being stuck with stock when demand collapses. Planning periodic relaunches fits a fashion product, and a long education campaign fits a high-learning product.

stem: Which list correctly names the four PLC extension strategies?
options: Deletion, harvesting, repositioning, line extension
Market penetration, market development, product development, diversification
Modifying the product, modifying the market, repositioning the product, introducing a new product
Product improvement, line extension, trading up, trading down
explanation: The four ways to extend a PLC are modifying the product, modifying the market, repositioning the product and introducing a new product. Market penetration, market development, product development and diversification form the strategic approaches to growth (Ansoff) matrix, and product improvement, line extension, trading up and trading down are sub-tactics, not the four strategies.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four strategies for extending a product's life cycle?
options: Modifying the market
Harvesting the product
Repositioning the product
Introducing a new product
explanation: Harvesting is a decline-stage strategy that accepts falling sales and cuts support; it does not extend the PLC. Modifying the market, repositioning and introducing a new product are three of the four extension strategies (modifying the product is the fourth).

stem: Brisk Bottling's mature iced-tea brand (1) adds a peach flavour, (2) promotes the tea to seniors, a group that never bought it, and (3) upgrades its ingredients and raises its price to position it as premium. Which extension strategies are these, in order?
options: Modifying the product; modifying the market; repositioning
Modifying the market; modifying the product; repositioning
Repositioning; modifying the market; introducing a new product
Modifying the product; repositioning; modifying the market
explanation: Adding a flavour is a line extension (modifying the product); reaching seniors is finding new customers (modifying the market); upgrading and raising the price is trading up (repositioning). Mixing up the flavour move (product) and the seniors move (market) is the most common error.

stem: Why do marketers use PLC extension strategies?
options: To reduce the array of new-product ideas to a manageable list
To test a product in a limited area before launch
To create primary demand for a brand-new product class
To keep a product from sliding into decline by finding new sources of sales
explanation: Extension strategies stretch a product's life, usually in maturity, by changing the product, the market or the positioning, or by replacing it with a new product. Narrowing ideas and test marketing are NPD-process steps, not life-cycle extension.

stem: As sales of its fifth-generation tablet flatten, TechNorth launches a sixth-generation model designed to replace it and carry its customers forward. Which PLC extension strategy is this?
options: Introducing a new product
Harvesting
Finding new customers
Trading down
explanation: Replacing an ageing product with a new one is the fourth extension strategy, introducing a new product. Harvesting is tempting because the old model is fading, but harvesting keeps the old product with reduced support instead of replacing it.

stem: Altering a product's characteristics, such as its quality, performance or appearance, to increase sales is called:
options: market modification
product modification
repositioning
market penetration
explanation: Changing the product itself (quality, performance, appearance) is product modification, which includes product improvements and line extensions. Market modification leaves the product unchanged and changes who uses it or how it's used.

stem: ClearView, a Canadian window-cleaner brand, reformulates its existing spray so it no longer streaks in freezing temperatures and relaunches it as 'new and improved'. This PLC extension tactic is:
options: a line extension
creating a new use situation
a product improvement
trading down
explanation: Upgrading the performance of the existing item is a product improvement, one form of product modification. It is not a line extension, because no new item was added to the line; the same spray was made better.

stem: Glacier Gum (a) reformulates its mint gum so the flavour lasts longer and (b) adds a new watermelon flavour to the line. Which is correct?
options: (a) product improvement; (b) line extension; both are product modifications
(a) is a line extension and (b) is a product improvement
(a) is a market modification and (b) is a product modification
Both are brand extensions, because the brand name stays the same
explanation: Improving an existing item is a product improvement; adding a new flavour to the line is a line extension. Both change the product, so both are product modifications. A brand extension would take the Glacier name into a new product class, which neither move does.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a form of product modification?
options: Improving a product's performance
Adding a new size to an existing line
Promoting an existing product to a new age group
Changing a product's appearance
explanation: Promoting the same product to a new age group is finding new customers, a market modification. Improving performance, changing appearance and adding a new size (a line extension) all modify the product.

stem: Sales of Prairie Peak's mature ski wax are slipping because competitors' waxes perform better in very cold snow. Which PLC extension option directly addresses this problem?
options: Creating a new use situation for the existing wax
Harvesting the wax to reap its remaining profit
Test marketing the existing wax in two cities
A product improvement that boosts cold-snow performance
explanation: The problem is the product's performance, so a product improvement (product modification) fixes it directly. Creating a new use situation would change how the wax is used without closing the performance gap, and harvesting gives up on growth.
